Actinic cheilitis is the most likely diagnosis given its predilection for the vermilion border of the lower lip, chronicity, and frequent lack of symptoms until late stages; it carries high malignant potential and warrants biopsy. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) must be strongly considered — up to 20% of actinic cheilitis cases progress to SCC, and early invasive or in situ SCC can be entirely asymptomatic. Verruca vulgaris is less common on lips but possible, especially with history of oral contact or immunosuppression; typically more exophytic and shorter duration, but persistence can occur. Lichen planus may present as a white, reticulated, or atrophic plaque on the lip and can be asymptomatic, though often associated with other mucosal or cutaneous findings. Granuloma fissuratum is a reactive fibrous hyperplasia usually linked to chronic mechanical trauma (e.g., ill-fitting dentures), but lower lip involvement is rare and typically symptomatic or associated with clear irritant exposure — making it the least likely without corroborating history."}
